# Online Supervised Learning

Up to this point we have talked about training a machine learning model once, using a fixed dataset, after which the model is deployed for its intended task. 

*Online learning*, on the other hand, updates the machine learning model incrementally as new data arrive, allowing it to adapt to changing patterns in real-time. 
This helps maintain model relevance in dynamic environments, and is also useful for large or streaming datasets where storing and retraining on all past data is impractical.

To fix ideas, we can precisely formulate an online supervised learning task:

:::{#def-online-ml-task}
### Online Supervised Learning Task
Fix sets $\mathcal{X}$, $\mathcal{Y}$, and $\mathcal{Z}$, a loss function $L : \mathcal{Y} \times \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, and a time horizon $T \in \mathbb{N}$.
At time $t+1$ we have access to data $\{(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{y}_i)\}_{i=1}^t$ where each $(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{y}_i)$ is a sample from an (unknown) distribution $P_t$.
The aim is to find a function $f : \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$ for which the *cumulative loss*
$$
\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{E}[ L(\mathbf{y}_t,f(\mathbf{x}_t)) ] 
$$ 
is minimal.
:::

@def-online-ml-task is deliberately vague about where the sequence of data-generating distributions $P_t$ might come from; there are two main situations to consider

1. **No feedback:** The sequence of distributions $P_t$ arise from some natural process that is unaffected by our actions; e.g. whether or not I carry an umbrella on day $t$ can be modelled as a Bernoulli distribution $P_t = \mathrm{Bern}(\rho_t)$ whose success parameter $\rho_t$ depends in turn on the weather on day $t$, which we do not control.
2. **Feedback:** The distribution $P_t$ may depend on the actions that we took in the past. For example, the probability $\rho_t$ that my friend will lend me an umbrella is likely to decrease if I keep asking to borrow their umbrella.

The simplest example of online machine learning without feedback is called the *bandit*, which we are going to meet in @sec-bandits.

Online machine learning with feedback is such a rich topic that we cannot hope to cover it in this module, but we give a passing nod to *reinforcement learning*, one of the main methods that address this task, in @sec-rl.


## Bandits {#sec-bandits}

Slot machines are also known pejoratively as *one-armed bandits*, alluding to the large mechanical levers affixed to the sides of early mechanical machines (cf. \Cref{fig: bandit}), and to the games' ability to empty players' pockets and wallets as thieves would.

At time $t$ the player inserts a coin (say $\pounds 1$), pulls the lever, and receives a random *reward* $\pounds R_t$ which has expectation $\mu \geq 0$ and is independent of all other rewards that have been received.
Their average expected reward after playing $T$ rounds is simply the expected reward $\mu$ from the bandit, i.e.
$$
\mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T R_t \right] = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{E}[R_t] = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mu = \mu ,
$$
So far, so straightforward.
The complication comes in when there is more than one bandit (we call this situation a *multi-armed bandit*), since the player must then select, at time $t$, which bandit to play next.
This is non-trivial when not all bandits are equal; the expected reward $\mu_i$ from the $i$th bandit may not be the same as the expected reward $\mu_j$ from another bandit ($j \neq i$), and the actual values of the $\mu_i$ will be unknown to the player in general.
Supposing there are $B$ bandits in total, the aim is then to minimise the *regret*
$$ 
 \mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T R_t , \qquad \mu_\star = \max_{1 \leq i \leq B} \mu_i ,    
$${#eq-bandit-regret}
where $R_t$ denotes the reward received at time $t \in \{1,\dots,T\}$.
If a player was lucky enough to only play the bandit with highest expected reward $\mu_\star$, then the player would have no expected regret:
$$
\mathbb{E}\left[ \mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T R_t \right] 
= \mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{E}[ R_t] 
= \mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mu_{\star} = 0 
$$
However, only by experimenting with each bandit, and potentially losing money in the process, can the player hope to truly discover which bandit provides the highest expected reward.

Though the terminology is inherited from gambling, multi-arm bandits appear in diverse application areas.
For example, in online advertising the advertiser would like to dynamically select which among a selection of different advertisements maximises click-through rates, or in sequential clinical trials one seeks to allocate treatments to maximise patient welfare with only a partial understanding of which treatments are effective at the outset.

Multi-arm bandits can be seen as a special case of the general online supervised learning task (cf. @def-online-ml-task) by taking $\mathcal{X} = \emptyset$, $\mathcal{Z} \in \{1,\dots,B\}$ indexes the bandits that can be played, $\mathbf{y}_t = (R_t^{(1)} , \dots , R_t^{(B)})$ are the rewards that would have been paid by each bandit at time $t$, and $L(\mathbf{y}_t , f) = - [\mathbf{y}_t]_f = - R_t^{(f)}$.
In particular, the regret @eq-bandit-regret is consistent with the notion of regret that we saw earlier in @eq-regret.

Although there is some redundancy in talking about both losses and rewards, the "reward" terminology feels much more natural in the bandit context, so we will use it.


::: {.remark #rem-context-bandit}
### Contextual Bandit[{{< fa star >}}{{< fa star >}}]{.advanced title="Non-Examinable content"}

A natural extension of the multi-arm bandit, which we will not consider in this module, is when the output from the bandit depends also on observable covariates $\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathcal{X}$.

For example, in a clinical trial we may know that patients with a specific genetic trait are more likely to respond well to a particular treatment, and we can use this information to help decide to which arm of the trial they are assigned.

This is known as a *contextual* bandit, with $\mathbf{x}_t$ representing the *context*.
:::

![A row of classical *bandit* machines, on display at Wookey Hole Caves in Somerset, England. Since there are four bandits, we call this setting a *4-armed bandit*.. [[source](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=4828058)]](figures/bandit.jpeg){#fig-bandit width=70%}

The reason that multi-arm bandits are non-trivial is because the player must balance two competing objectives; *exploration*, to find out which bandit provides the highest expected reward, and *exploitation*, to repeatedly play the machine that is believed to provide the highest expected reward. This is known as an **exploration-exploitation trade-off**.

Let's examine the two edge cases in turn:


### Pure Exploration {#sec-pure-exploration}

If we want to learn as much as we can about the vector $\bm{\mu} = (\mu_1,\dots,\mu_B)$ of expected rewards, then an intuitively reasonable strategy is to spend an equal amount of time playing each bandit.
The expected regret is then
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}\left[ \mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T R_t  \right] & = \mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{E}[R_t] \\
& = \mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^B \mu_i \\
& = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^B (\mu_\star - \mu_i) 
\end{align*}
$$
which does not vanish (assuming the $\mu_i$ are not all equal) as $T \rightarrow \infty$; we always have some regret if we play a pure exploitation strategy!

### Pure Exploitation {#sec-pure-exploitation}

The opposite of exploration is to repeatedly play the machine that we believe has the highest expected reward.
Of course, we know nothing at the outset, so let's suppose we allocate the first $T_0$ attempts to performing some form of exploration, enabling us to estimate the vector $\bm{\mu}$ of expected rewards from these data, say using $\hat{\bm{\mu}}$.
Thereafter we will continue to play any bandit which maximises $i \mapsto \hat{\mu}_i$.
Since the exploration dataset has finite size $T_0$, we cannot expect $\hat{\bm{\mu}}$ to be in exact agreement with $\bm{\mu}$; as such, there is a positive probability that
$$
\argmax_{1 \leq i \leq B} \hat{\mu}_i \notin \argmax_{1 \leq i \leq B} \mu_i ,
$$
and we will go on to indefinitely play a sub-optimal bandit.
Let $\gamma = 1$ if this event occurs, and otherwise $\gamma = 0$.
Let $\rho = \mathbb{E}[\gamma]$ be the probability of this event, and let 
$$
\Delta = \mu_\star - \max\left\{ \mu_i : \mu_i \neq \mu_\star \right\}
$$
be the difference in expectation between the best bandit(s) and the second best bandit(s).
Then
$$
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}\left[ \mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T R_t  \right] 
    & = \underbrace{ \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T_0} \mathbb{E}[ \mu_\star -  R_t ] }_{\rightarrow 0 \text{ as } T \rightarrow \infty} + \underbrace{ \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=T_0+1}^T \mathbb{E}[ \mu_\star - R_t]  }_{(*)}
\end{align*}
$$
where, using the tower property of conditional expectation,
$$
\begin{align*}
    (\star) & = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t = T_0 + 1}^T \mathbb{E}[ \mathbb{E}[ \mu_\star - R_t | \gamma] ] 
    \geq \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t = T_0 + 1}^T [ (1 - \rho) \times 0 + \rho \times \Delta ] 
    = \frac{\rho}{T} \sum_{t=T_0+1}^T \Delta 
\end{align*}
$$
which does not vanish as $T \rightarrow \infty$.
Thus we are not much better off than the pure exploration strategy in @sec-pure-exploration; we have non-vanishing expected regret.

### $\epsilon$-greedy {#sec-epsilon-greedy}

From @sec-pure-exploration and @sec-pure-exploitation, it is intuitively clear that neither pure exploration or pure exploitation are satisfactory; given an infinite number of attempts, we ought to be able to eventually identify the bandit paying the highest expected reward and then exploit it.
That is, there ought to be a mixed strategy, involving both exploration and exploitation, for which we have asymptotically vanishing regret.
Such strategies do indeed exist and are not unique; in this section we consider a particularly simple idea called the *$\epsilon$-greedy* method.

The idea behind $\epsilon$-greedy is that we eventually want to have accurate estimates for the vector $\bm{\mu}$ of average rewards, but we only want to devote a small proportion $\epsilon$ of our playing to achieve this goal.

To operationalise this, we can imagine that at each time $t$ we "flip an $\epsilon$ coin" to decide whether to play a bandit selected uniformly at random (i.e. with probability $\epsilon$ we explore by playing a random bandit), or to play the bandit we currently believe to be the best (i.e. with probability $1 - \epsilon$ we exploit our current knowledge to play what we believe is most likely to be the best bandit).

Let's calculate our expected regret under the $\epsilon$-greedy method.
Let $\gamma_t$ be the event that our belief about which is the best bandit is incorrect at time $t$ and let $\rho_t = \mathbb{E}[\gamma_t]$.
Using again the tower property of conditional expectation, this time we derive an upper bound
$$
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}\left[ \mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T R_t  \right] 
        & = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{E}[\mu_\star - \mathbb{E}[R_t | \gamma_t]  ]
        \leq \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \rho_t \Delta
\end{align*}
$$
which vanishes as $T \rightarrow \infty$ whenever $\rho_t \rightarrow 0$ as $t \rightarrow \infty$.
In other words, as long as we eventually learn which is the best bandit, we will have asymptotically zero regret.

A simple strategy to learn the best bandit is to let $\hat{\mu}_i$ be the average of the rewards that we have obtained from the $i$th bandit at time $t$; from Hoeffding's inequality (\Cref{lem: Hoeffding}) we know that each $\hat{\mu}_i$ converges to $\mu_i$ in probability as the total number of plays of the $i$th bandit is increased, and from this we can deduce that $\rho_t$, the probability of selecting a sub-optimal bandit, becomes vanishingly small.
 

## Reinforcement Learning {#sec-rl}

The challenge of online supervised learning is markedly increased when our actions at time $t$ can affect future outcomes; i.e. in the presence of feedback.
An important example of this is a *Markov decision process*, where the *states* $(\mathbf{x}_t)_{t \geq 1}$ evolve as a Markov chain, and $\mathbf{x}_{t+1}$ is allowed to depend on the *action* $f(\mathbf{x}_t)$ that we take at time $t$.

The study of how to select a *policy* $f(\cdot)$ to minimise regret is called *reinforcement learning*. All of the previous considerations from @sec-bandits apply here; we also are faced with an exploration-exploitation trade-off, since we want to both find and exploit an optimal policy $f(\cdot)$.

![The first 99 moves in AlphaGo (white) v. Tang Weixing (31 December 2016). [[source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AlphaGo)]](figures/go.png){#fig-go width=70%}


::: {#exm-alphago}
### AlphaGo

Go, an abstract strategy board game for two players in which the aim is to fence off more territory than the opponent, was invented in China more than 2,500 years ago (@fig-go). A decade or so ago many people believed that computers would not be able to compete with the most skilled human players at Go. 

This was not an unreasonable belief; the most powerful chess engines were exploiting tree search to explore the consequences of a large number of moves several steps ahead, but by comparison the combinatorial complexity of Go would render tree search impractical.

This all changed with *AlphaGo*, which in 2016 defeated one of the world’s top professional players @silver2016mastering.

AlphaGo was in effect a demonstration of the potential of reinforcement learning, showing how this enables a computer to evaluate board positions and anticipate future moves with remarkable precision. 

Let's see how this online supervised learning task is formulated:

*  The state $\mathbf{x}_t$ represents the current configuration of the Go board, including the positions of all black and white stones, whose turn it is, and any additional game-specific information (for Go aficionados, this includes *ko* situations).
*  The policy $f(\cdot)$ is constructed using a deep neural network and tells us where to place our next stone on the board[^alphago-comment]. 
*  The next state $\mathbf{x}_{t+1}$ is obtained from the current state $\mathbf{x}_t$ and the action $f(\mathbf{x}_t)$. For Go this is fully deterministic; placing a stone on a legal point leads to a new board configuration (with any captures resolved).
*  AlphaGo used a *sparse* reward, with $R_t = 0$ for all intermediate moves and either $R_t = 1$ or $–1$ at the end of the game, depending on whether the game was won or lost. 

:::

The field of reinforcement learning is moving fast.
For example, the performance of AlphaGo has been superseded by a general-purpose machine learning tool for game-playing called *MuZero* @schrittwieser2020mastering.


[^alphago-comment]:
    Of course we are glossing over details here; for example, in AlphaGo a *stochastic* policy was actually used.
